We saw on two bridges that were photographed from the direction looking towards the church and then from the church to the other side when Munira Zametica last her life when trying to get some water from the Dorinja stream. The documents that you read, did they indicate that there was shooting from both sides at that place and at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Witness Sadija Sahinovic even stated that she and Munira Zametica wondered whether they should go or not because shooting was heard; and when they went to the bridge, the shooting was also ongoing. Several people were there. They were hiding behind the pillar of the bridge and occasionally they would go to fetch water. Also when Munira Zametica got killed, then - according to the testimony of this witness - two soldiers of the BiH army shot towards the church from the bridge in order to make it possible for the people to get Munira Zametica from the river. So that was her opinion. And, in any case, there was shooting going on, on that day; but no one defined precisely who was shooting and from where - this is not known, just that there was shooting going on in the area. And according to the testimony of this witness, she noticed that the bullets fell into the bed of the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you now tell us what your conclusion is concerning this incident.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, Munira Zametica was shot by two bullets, two projectiles; one hit her in the chest. She then straightened out and put her hands on her chest and then she was hit by another bullet. It -- there was a very short interval between these two instances. And if we take into account that Munira Zametica was trying to reach for water, so she was not standing straight up ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could you again -- the witness is including the evaluation of the totality of the evidence; that's not for the witness to do. I told that yesterday to you. This witness can comment on any matter that pertains to his expertise, not on whether there was time between this and that, unless it has a direct bearing on his expertise, in which case he can explain to us what that is. But the witness is, as a matter of fact, writing our judgement -- at least suggesting at what we should conclude, whereas the witness should be limited to his field of expertise. Would you please - I told this to you yesterday - I again remind you of that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, my question was: What was the conclusion of this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You asked him for further conclusion, yes, of course you did. And the witness had explained before what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- [Overlapping speakers] conclusions, right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Hmm?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As an expert, he should have conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, in his field of expertise, not in evaluating what is credible evidence, whether we could believe that there was two seconds between this, not whether the shooting from the other side was in time in response, et cetera; that's all outside his field of expertise. And the witness therefore asking whatever conclusions he draws on the basis of his expertise and then explain what exactly that basis is and on what facts that is based, and the basis could not be the evaluation of this witness of which is -- what is more or less credible in the evidence. So therefore, please keep this in mind. And this is not the beginning of a debate. This is guidance for you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Poparic, you have heard both my question and the concern of the Trial Chamber, concerning whether you're analysing anything.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's a misunderstanding, but let me tell you first what my conclusion is. It is that this victim, if she was targeted from the direction of the church in Veljena at the distance of 1100 metres, considering the size of the victim and the two shots that she sustained, she could only have been hit with semi-automatic sniper rifle, 7.9-millimetre which has the least dispersion, though it's very difficult for the marksman to achieve two hits at such a short distance considering the characteristics of this weapon and the usual dispersion. In my view, it's much more probable that Munira Zametica was killed by a burst of fire, that is to say, most probably a burst of fire spread across the bed of the river and, because of the concrete bed of the river, the bullets ricochetted. The characteristics of the river-bed is such that the ricochet becomes directed into one and the same direction. This is how she could have been hit by two bullets. So in my view, most probably it was some sort of burst of fire from which she was hit by two shots on the said occasion. It's very unlikely that it was an automatic rifle, because if we take into account the size of the victim and the distance and all the other circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there anywhere in the materials you read, is there any witness who talked not about individual shots but about a burst of fire? Did you find that anywhere supported by any of the witnesses, witness statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No one said that these were either single shots or bursts of fire. There are just statements that there were bullets falling around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If there was a burst of fire -- or let me first ask you this. Except the church which can be seen in the photographs, was there any other building on the Serb side from which it could be shot at this area?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at this particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is the likelihood that Munira Zametica would be hit by a burst of fire coming from the church, that she would be intentionally targeted?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's very difficult to assess. It could be an accidental hit, but I reached the conclusion that most probably it was a burst of fire because if it was a longer burst of fire and if it hit the river-bed and the wall, it is always directed in one direction. She must have been exposed to a series of bullets, and that was why she was hit by two shots. To be hit by two shots in such a short interval from a sniper rifle or even a burst of fire if it was intentional, the likelihood would be very small; it's possible but very unlikely. Because we have to take into account that the sniper rifle is intended for shooting up to the distance of 800 metres - that's not a problem for a good marksman to hit a target - but if the dance is greater, then one needs to be both a very good marksman and highly concentrated and some time is needed also for all the elements to be in place for a hit. So in my view, the likelihood that she was intentionally targeted and then hit by sniper fire is extremely small.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to put one question for clarification. To one of the previous sentences -- questions, you answered, Witness: "Not at this particular time." And the question was: "Was there any other building on the Serb side from which it could be shot at this area?" Can you explain a bit further? What kind of buildings at that relevant time had been there? And what changes have been made the last 20 years? Or how do I have to understand your answer "not at this particular time," with respect to buildings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time of the incident, there was a church in the area still under construction; later on, it was finished. Yesterday we have shown you photograph 63, where you could see a number of other buildings that were built a few years ago, maybe five or six. In any case, they are new buildings and they are marked on the photograph with the X's, and there is the building number 4, which is a bit further away from the church; at the time, they were not there. There was only a hill at the time that was rather empty. There was nothing else there, save for the church.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we next move to page 100 in the B/C/S of -- in your report and 98 in the English. It is incident F-4 of the 3rd of September, 1993. It is stated that Nafa Taric and her 8-year-old daughter were shot and wounded by a single bullet while crossing Ivana Krndelja Street in the Hrasno neighbourhood in Sarajevo." In your view, how did the incident develop and what do the documents say plus what were the basic concerns you had to deal with first to shed light on the events?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, according to the statement of this witness, she was crossing Ivana Krndelja Street, where at the time there were containers blocking the view from Hrasno and Ozrenska Street; they sheltered herself and her daughter. When she crossed the street and passed the containers, she made another step, when she was hit by a projectile which hit not only her but her daughter as well. The basic problem was to determine where she could have been visible from and whether she could have been hit from the direction of Ozrenska Street. It was established that there was a position indeed in Ozrenska Street held by the VRS; it is some 800-plus metres away. The closest point along the separation line was at 680 metres. We established the separation line based on a map of the ABiH. Also, given the specificities of the terrain, one could still approximately determine where the positions had been and where the line stood. Since she indicated how the event happened and which path she crossed between the shelter and the place where she was hit, it was possible to determine how much time the shooter needed to spot her and hit her. Our conclusion was that if we take the closest point, that is to say, 680 metres from which she was fired at, the shooter must have fired before he could see her in order for the bullet to hit her in that location. As for the distance of 800-plus metres, the time required would be even greater. At the distance of 680 metres, at that spot we could not determine whether there was any visibility of the place where the incident happened, that is to say, from that position. As for the other position where the trenches of the VRS were at 800 metres, the place where she was shot was visible though. The basic conclusion is that the shooter would have had to fire the shot before he could see Nafa Taric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I ask you: Wouldn't that fully depend on the speed with which she crossed the area where she was visible and how large that area exactly was? Would you agree with me that that would be determining for your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First, what could you tell us exactly about the time it took her to go from the one sheltered area, to cross the open area, and then how much time exactly did she take to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She spent 1.2 seconds out of cover, according to her statement; and the projectile would have had to travel that time if it was fired from the M84 machine-gun, which has the shortest flight time of projectile. So the shooter would have had to fire 0.2 seconds before he saw Nafa Taric without even calculating in the time that one would need to acquire a target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, what time would the bullet need to travel the 800 metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not 800 metres, 680.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We chose the closest position at the separation line, 680 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would it -- how much time would --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1.2 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, how long - that was my first question - how long did she take to cross that open space? Was she there for half a second? Was she there for 3 seconds? Was she there for -- perhaps the child not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1.2 seconds. She was on the move, so let's take the time of 1.2 seconds. She was already moving, if you understand me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll stop you there. "Let's take the 1.2 seconds" is not what I'm interested in. What I'm interested in is: How long was she there, visible, between the containers? Do you have any knowledge about that? No assumptions, but whether it took her 1 second, 3 seconds, whether perhaps the child was not very willing to come with her? Yes, do you know --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She could not be seen while behind the container. Once she cleared the container, she was hit and she indicated as much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How long was she visible, exposed, when she had cleared the container?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1.02 seconds. 1 second and 200th parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I measured it. She indicated that. She took the steps and I measured the time. There's footage, so it was a kind of reconstruction of the event. She walked from the place of the container to the place where she was hit. She made perhaps one step or a bit more before she was hit. That is her statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you say the speed at the reconstruction must have been exactly the same as at the time. You consider this to be sufficient for such far-reaching conclusions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Her speed was probably not -- as I tried to tell you, she set out -- it wasn't the same. She started moving from a stop position, and it took a bit to acquire speed. If she was already on the move behind the container originally, then that time to cross the distance would have been even shorter because she had this initial speed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're not answering my question. My question was: Whether the reconstruction would create such a position that by the hundredths of a second, you would be able to draw conclusions? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the time I measured. I did not want to correct it. But the difference between the two would be 0.18 seconds, almost 2 seconds. It's not such a short time for such a short distance. If she was mistaken, then that's a different thing; but I'm saying that I calculated it on the basis of her statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But if, for example, the child was keeping her slightly back, that might have taken another half a second or perhaps one second. Have you considered that possibility, indeed, that the reconstruction did not in detail -- is suitable for such precise timing exercises?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't my reconstruction but the reconstruction of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What I'm saying is: You apparently found the reconstruction sufficiently precise up to the one- or two-hundredths of a second to draw such conclusions as far-reaching as you did? Could you please answer that question, not any other one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given the very short distance she covered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, could you answer my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to answer. Given the very short distance, I am convinced that the time measured is accurate. So the difference is not in two-hundredths parts, but 0.18, almost 0.2 seconds. For such a short distance, it is quite accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've not answered my question. You're pointing at the accuracy of your time measurement, and I am pointing at -- possibly at a slight difference between what happened at the incident itself and what happened during the reconstruction. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I? Just one clarification. You -- once you answered the question, saying it was 1.2 seconds; and some lines further down, you said 1.02 seconds. Which of the two is true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1.02 seconds, that is the time I measured that Ms. Nafa Taric needed to move from the container to the place where she was hit; 1.2 seconds is the time needed by a projectile to cover the distance from the closest point at the separation line to the place where she was hit. So the difference between the two is 0.18 seconds. And in my view, given the short distance she covered, it is accurate enough. She may have well covered a distance of 2 metres, but she didn't say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I put on the record that three times you were asked about the time the witness was in the open, to be seen by a possible shooter; and you three times answered "1.2 seconds." I just put it on the record. It's on page 24 and 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I've another question for you. You said --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we will verify --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- this was translation issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There may be a translation issue. If there is a translation issue, we'll resolve that and then it will be clear. The timing of it -- how much time was taken to leave the cover and to enter -- or at the place where she was hit, how did you measure that? Did you do that by -- what kind of instrument did you use to measure the time which you said was 1.02 seconds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a programme for film editing which specifies the precise time in hundredth parts of a second; that is what I used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it is very accurate. The programme measures it very accurately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And how accurate was exactly the point where she said she was hit? I mean, was that also by the one-hundredth of a second precise that you could say "here she was hit" in the reconstruction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I didn't quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you mean the distance or time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If in a reconstruction you move from a place to a place where you say you were hit, how accurately can you determine exactly by a hundredth of a second where it was, where you were when you were hit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She indicated it. I did not establish the place where she was hit. She covered the distance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and I measured the time. I was not the one to determine where she was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How did she indicate the place where she was hit? Did she say that? I know that it's in in evidence before us, but I'm asking you. Did she say that or was it where she stopped or -- do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She stopped at that place and then Mr. Barry Hogan marked it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you say it took her 1.02 seconds exactly to reach that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is what I measured, on the footage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then, again, when you stop, if I stop a movement, that takes in itself one-tenth or two-tenths of a second. If I say -- If I take something and I stop, that in itself is a -- there's already quite some discussion possible as to whether it was here or here. How did you determine exactly where she stopped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I measured the time when she stopped, when she was no longer moving, that is. So the time that you referred to is included in this time. But as I've already said, as she set out she lost a bit of time, because she did not have any initial velocity, she was moving in reality. So the distance was shorter. I thought that that should not be corrected at all because I took into account that perhaps she had set out so this would be compensated in some way. So her time was approximately what was measured. Actually, the time of her movement is the time that I measured, taking into account everything that you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's clear what you're -- how you reached your conclusions. Please proceed, Mr. -- no, I'm looking at the clock. We should not proceed at all. We take a break, and we will resume at five minutes past 11.00. Mr. Poparic, you may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome back, Witness. Judge Fluegge has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to take you back to page 25, lines 15 to 18 of today's transcript and I read it to you. "I measured it." And it was in relation to a question of Judge Orie, how do you know the time, 1.02 seconds. You said: "I measured it. She indicated that. She took the steps and I measured the time. There's footage, so it was a kind of reconstruction of the event. She walked from the place of the container to the place where she was hit." I'm not quite sure. It could be understood that you personally have been at the spot of the event together with the witness. Have you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the reconstruction took place, I think, in 2001 in the presence of the Prosecutor, Barry Hogan. It's a Prosecution film.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you take from that footage that the witness was asked to walk the same speed as -- during the situation where she was hit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, she was not given any kind of instructions. She walked from the place where the end of the container was to the place where she was hit, and then she naturally walked up to there. She did not get any instructions to reconstruct the speed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And this is the only basis for your conclusion that she walked 1.02 seconds; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And was the container still there so you could determine very precisely where exactly the open spot was and where the container was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the container wasn't there. She indicated where the container had been and how many steps she had taken from the container. So my understanding was that she indicated that on the basis of her recollection as to how many steps she had taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Mr. Lukic, I'm just wondering whether that reconstruction -- we know that there are a few in evidence. Do you know whether this one falls -- it's not a D --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's my next question and it's not in evidence yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not in evidence. So we listening to a lot of comments on matters which are not yet in evidence. Well, then the most appropriate thing to do is to first -- because I was searching where it was so that we could better understand the testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 22311E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I give you as guidance for the next time to first introduce that and say: Witness, is this the basis on which you made your calculations? And then so that -- because I desperately tried to find it because we -- I know it, we have it from the football match, we have that Barry Hogan video, that's, I think, D382; we have another one, I think, D381; D385. But I was desperately trying to better understand the testimony of the witness. It's better that we have seen the basis on which he drew his conclusions and not the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was afraid that it might be leading. That's why I was first -- I first asked the witness and then my intention is to show this video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you could explain that, but there are ways to make it not leading, but please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We will she now 65 ter 22311E which is ERN number V000-6006-1. We will see this video from time 3:35 until -- or sorry, 3 minutes, 38 seconds, up to 5 minutes, 09 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you please give the 65 ter number again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's 65 ter number 22311E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is 15-minute clip from the larger video, but now we will see only two minutes, minute and a half. And we will have Barry Hogan speaking in English, and there is a translation, B/C/S translation. There will be some traffic, so maybe -- I think it -- still it would be audible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Otherwise we would have to stop that traffic, isn't it, Mr. Lukic? Have the transcripts been provided to the booths? And is it the first time we play it or is it -- has it been played before? I see the booths are --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, we did not provide the transcript to the booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it should be played -- no even playing twice because the first round is always to check whether the transcript corresponds with -- but if there's no transcript then --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is no transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest that the disadvantages for the public and for the Defence, because Mr. Mladic will not be able to hear it --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is translation on the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: B/C/S translation as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Yes, because Mr. Hogan is speaking English and then perhaps that would resolve the problem. Apologies for being too eager on that. Let's play the video and let's have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But we start at 3:38 not 3:35, as you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was corrected by my colleague. Can we play it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "THE INVESTIGATOR: Could you please stand at the place where, to the best of your recollection, the edge of the barricade was located on the day that you were shot. "NAFA TARIC: [Indicates] "THE INVESTIGATOR: I will mark this location with yellow spray paint. Can you please indicate with your hand which area from this location was open. "NAFA TARIC: [Indicates] "THE INVESTIGATOR: Could you please now stand at the spot where, to the best of your recollection, you were when you were wounded. "NAFA TARIC: [Indicates] "THE INVESTIGATOR: I will now mark the spot, with yellow spray paint, the figure 'X,' with the number '1' beside it. "Would you please show me, to the best of your recollection, where your daughter was located when she was shot. "NAFA TARIC: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Poparic, you were asked whether this is the only basis for your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is footage on the basis of which I measured that Ms. Nafa Taric walked from the container to the place where she was hit and it was 1 second, point --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear you, so could you please finish.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not understand. Before ...

utterances.text: But you measured her step and not anything else? In time, I mean. You measured the time for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I mean, there's nothing else I could have measured; right? Just that, that movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now let's just assume it's 20 centimetres wrong. What would be the whole distance approximately she moved with this one step?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was not what I asked. I asked what would be the total distance with this one step.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, if she's 20 centimetres away from the original point covered by the container, that would then be 25 percent of the total distance, or 20 per cent, depending on where you start. Would you agree with that?

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why do you think it's one-hundredth of a second if for the whole of the distance you need one second, why would 25 percent take only 1 per cent extra time? Any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't say that. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you said would -- I think you would have -- you said that it makes one-hundredth of a -- or one-tenth -- let me check what the transcript exactly says. One second, please. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 0.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 0.1, that's one one-tenth. Yes, it says less than 0.01 seconds, which is one-hundredth. We'll check at the audio what you said. utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then the time would be more, considerably. I mean, if she took one more step, then it's roughly another second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if, for example, you take two steps of 60 centimetres, which is not abnormal, you end up at the same point, at 1 metre, 20 approximately - a little bit over 1 metre - and that would have considerably changed the time needed, you say. utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

It is well-known and that is in the rules, 30 bullets per second, that is the speed -- the firing speed. So well-trained shooter would achieve that. So he would need -- no, not seconds, minutes. Sorry. Sorry, was I saying "seconds"? A well-trained shooter needs, say, 2 seconds for every bullet. Let us assume that we have a super-trained shooter and that he needs much less time, say, 1 second. In my view, I accept all of this thinking and that's what I bore in mind when I was working on this. Again, it covers this time that the bullet had to be fired before the shooter saw the victim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you say 30 bullets a minute. Would that be true also for -- if you are prepared to shoot, knowing where you expect your target? That's different from 30 shots in a minute, because most of the initial time might have been spent already by --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I reduced the time to 1 second. I suppose that it was a well-trained marksman and that he would more or less expect that. But regardless of what he expected there, it's -- there is some time that he would need. There is a situation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... need for what? To pull the trigger? That's the only thing he needs to do, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, there is this claim that she was hit from the building of the Institute for the Blind. Maybe it would be useful if we would go back to that image. Perhaps it would be easier to follow if we had the image before us.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have to say that while the girls were at the incident site which is marked by number 5 in Djuro Jaksica Street, they were not visible from the Institute for the Blind which is marked with number 1. When they moved a little, here to the side street between the buildings marked by numbers 3 and 2, they became partly visible which can be seen in the video when Medina stands in front of the trench. Then in the corner one can see a part of one window of the Institute for the Blind. And I think that this was the basis for the claim that they were hit from there. However, we got photographs that were made in 1996 in a video, and one can see that that part of the Institute for the Blind was devastated and no sniper or sharpshooter could have been there; it was too dangerous. You can see that it was less than 100 metres the distance from the building marked with number 2 and the Institute for the Blind and probably it would have been very dangerous. The evidence -- or rather, the photographs from the relevant period from the territory under the control of the VRS show that the old people's home marked with number 4 here was also riddled with bullets and projectiles just like the building marked with number 2. The photograph is provided in this report. That indicates that the fire between the two warring parties was actually exchanged in the direction which I marked here with the line A. That's the most probable direction of the exchange of fire because the Institute for the Blind was too dangerous a place for anyone to be there. According to the photograph, there could have been some troops below the Institute for the Blind, but up there I don't think so. Then further, the incident was analysed because in the photograph that we got from the video, at the frontal side of the Institute for the Blind there are traces of some breaks of something like shape-charged projectiles. Could anyone shoot through these openings? All the analysis shows that in such a case the place would have had to be rearranged, a part of the wall had to be demolished, and so on, because the angle to the incident site in relation to the frontal wall of the Institute for the Blind is about 25 degrees. So for a marksman to be able to place a rifle there, a part of the wall had to be demolished and the firing position rearranged accordingly. No one ever presented evidence that there was a firing position there, though the place was inspected after the Dayton Accords. I never received anything that would indicate to me that that was an arranged firing position. So in my view, the exchange of fire was along the axis A and the ricochetting of a bullet against the building number 2 is what hit Sanela Muratovic. So in my view, this is the most probable chain of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Poparic, you have seen a Judge said he couldn't see the tram.

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said these were the passengers from the third tram which is further away in this image. And the two trams that were hit previously are somewhere behind the person who is filming this. The first one that was hit was close to the old tobacco factory, and the other two closer to the Executive Council building. So when the two were hit, then these passengers were walking and then the fire we just saw was opened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And where can we see one of the three trams in the still we have on the screen now, at 3:37?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here we can't see it, but there are some videos or shots where they can be seen too. For example, 141, image 140, in the report you can see the position of these trams. Tram 236, one can see that it stopped in front of the Executive Council building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How do you know that the people in the street then falling down came from one of the trams? How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And what makes you certain that those people we just saw in the video are the same referred to by the tram driver?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, ultimately it's not so important whether they came from the tram or not. They may just have happened to walk there. They were walking along the street, and then fire was opened. That's essential in my view, but I think that they did walk out of the tram -- or at least most of them did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If it's not important, why did you say that these are passengers from the tram?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I read the statement of the tram driver, that the tram stopped there, and it's logical that people continued to move on. When there are people in the street -- because there is not a residential area. There is a faculty building and the museum and so on. So this number of people, I suppose, that they originated from the tram.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. You suppose that, and in your view this is logical. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I have a further clarification, please. We see these people are shot not inside the tram but they're outside. What had made the tram driver to stop the tram to allow these people to come out in the first place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He may have seen that the other two trams in front of him were standing, and that's why he may have stopped; or perhaps somebody may have signalised this to him, but this I don't know. From the place where he was he could see that two other trams were standing still at a distance of around 100 metres between the other two. So he saw that there was some sort of a standstill, so that may have been a reason for him to stop, to allow the passengers to continue on foot. But maybe somebody had told him to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we go into private session for one moment, please, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. But it's also time for a break. Yes. We take a break and resume at quarter to 2.00. Witness, you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could I seek briefly clarification on one or two matters. Witness, when you were talking about sniping incident F-5, that was Ramiza Kundo going or to or coming from the well, on page 58, line 24, you said: "However, on the right-hand side there was territory under the control of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Now, approximately a page later, that's page 59, lines 24, 25, you said: "We're not understanding each other. She showed a concern direction and I say that informs that direction that there was positions of the VRS and the ABiH and we found that out from other sources." Now if I understood you well, first you said it was one side she showed that, that's Republika Srpska, and on the right-hand side there was territory under the control of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina - that would be opposite directions - whereas your later testimony, at least if I understood it well, suggests that there were positions of the VRS and the ABiH on the same side. Could you clarify the issue for me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there was some misunderstanding in the first translation or I wasn't clear. The positions of the ABiH and the VRS were on the same side in that meadow, in the direction indicated by the witness on the footage, it was down the street. If we are looking from the direction of the hill, on the right-hand side there were VRS positions; on the left-hand side, ABiH positions. Perhaps the misunderstanding was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I have one other matter. I think you said all the evidence hinted - and I am now talking about the trams - all the evidence hints at shots being fired from the BH Executive Council building. Could you tell me what evidence you had specifically on your mind when you said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I said that, I had in mind the footage that exists about the events - of which there are many; there are also many witness statements given to TV crews; then there are witness statements provided to the Prosecution or to the police; there are police reports, UNPROFOR reports containing much information which unambiguously indicates that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, could you perhaps make a short list of what sources make you say that all the evidence - you didn't say most of the evidence but all the evidence - so that we can check whether it is in evidence before us, yes or no. Because if you are, in general terms, referring to TV interviews, then I've got no idea whether that's in evidence before us. And my next question would be: Have you ever read any suggestion that the fire would have come from the Holiday Inn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We should see one video now first, it's 1D5931.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. If I may. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I did not know about it, but on a second thought I did. Perhaps a day or two later, there was a meeting between General Rose and General Mladic. At that meeting, General Mladic denied any responsibility on the VRS side, saying that the shots were fired from another side, from the Holiday Inn. So I apologise for not having mentioned that immediately. So I do know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So not all the evidence suggested the Executive Council building --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are correct. I wasn't precise enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there also evidence suggesting that it may have come from close to the Jewish cemetery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right, because I mentioned all evidence, but I should have said a lot of the evidence. I'm not a lawyer and I may be imprecise. There is an UNPROFOR report stating that the fire could have come from that direction, but we will probably come to that later; it is in my report. There are some elements which would confirm otherwise in the same report. The police report, of course, is also different. It does not contribute to my thesis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is there any evidence that points at the Metalka building, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are some such assertions, but no evidence, no proof. The police claim that it was fired from the Metalka building. An OTP expert also claimed that the shots came from the Metalka building. It's Mr. Van der Weijden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you say it's no evidence. Whatever is presented before this Chamber is in evidence. Therefore, since you said "all suggest that it came from," whereas I now pointed at three or four other sources mentioned - I'm not saying which one is right or which one is wrong - I'd like to know exactly what is at the basis of your assertion that all the evidence, or at least the evidence you referred to, hints at the building you mentioned. If you could please write it briefly down so that we are sure that we are not overlooking any important source of evidence which is before us. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I do have a follow-up question. You've just said here at page 76, lines 23 to 24 that: "The police report does not contribute to my thesis." As a result of it not contracting to your thesis, did you then consider that report or didn't you consider it as a possible explanation of where the firing could have come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. Of course, I considered it and I quoted it in several places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. So we'll see now video 1D05931. We'll see it from 1 hour, 35 minutes, 21 seconds, up to 1 hour, 35 minutes, 51 seconds. After that immediately we will see the same video from 1 hour, 41 minutes, and 49 seconds, up to 1 hour, 43 minutes. So let's start from the first part.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Stop. We stopped at 1 hour, 35 minutes, 32 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: 35 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I see 32 -- 35 minutes, yes, 32 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What could we see in this part of the footage, Mr. Poparic? Is this the tram? Is this the incident? Did you view there footage?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, it is tram number 236. Next to the door, closer to the window, we can see the shards of glass which was shattered on the tram. It is undisputable evidence that the tram was hit at that place. Several witnesses stated that when the tram was hit the driver stopped immediately, although they were telling him to keep going. It is very logical that the driver stopped because a bullet flew close to his head, hitting a pole close by. He was probably scared and stopped because of his instinct. So the tram was hit there, and the glass that shattered fell on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do all reports indicate that the tram was stopped here or that it stopped -- or actually that it was hit at a different place?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police report states that it was hit at the Metalka building. The OTP experts claim the same. In an UNPROFOR report, it is stated that it was hit around that location. They were not very precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can I ask you one thing. Do I understand that you say the glass on the ground indicates that that's where the tram was hit? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Not only the glass but also witness statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, if a tram drives at a speed of - well, what could it be? - 20, 30 kilometres an hour, how much would it take to come to a full stop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is, first of all, questionable whether the speed was 20 or 30 kilometres per hour. It would require high-quality rails. If it was 20 or 30, it could be calculated, although I can't do it off the top of my head. I would say 10 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 10 metres. Now if a bullet hits a window, would the glass particles also travel another 10 metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they would not, but there's a different situation here. The tram was hit with a burst of fire, several bullets. As I said, one of the bullets flew close to the driver, hitting a pole nearby. It was probably because of that bullet that he began braking, so it was already in the process of stopping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said: "Next to the door, closer to the window, we can see the shards of glass which was shattered on the tram. It is undisputable evidence that the tram was hit at that place." So as a matter of fact, you're saying that the tram was hit when it had already come to a full stop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It was probably in the process of stopping. It was being fired at and the driver probably stopped out of fear, by instinct. One doesn't need to be surprised to find the glass particles there. Had this glass pane been hit first, the particles would have probably been somewhere closer to the end of the tram, but in any case, it was around here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, is the -- you say the conclusion is because that's how it was. That sounds not very scientific. "Had this glass been hit first, the particles would have probably been somewhere closer to the end of the the tram, but in any case, it was around here." That is whatever you say, this is how it was, without further explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The far end of the tram.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What's -- okay. Let's move on. Mr. Lukic, please proceed. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we go further with any videos today, I'm just going back to 65 ter number 22533, that we watched a short fragment of before the break, at 3:30 to 3:37. And there was discussion about that and the witness testified he clearly relied on it. That's not been tendered. And if we're going on to other bits of videos after this one as well, I would suggest or recommend that this tiny clip should be tendered as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, are you intending to tender this clip?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not yet. As I said, we'll play another part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you'll finally tender it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will finally tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So can we proceed with this part, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, would you mind to replay it from the beginning so that I have a better -- a more vivid recollection of what we saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Give us one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And Ms. Edgerton asked you if you are going to tender 65 ter 22533.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I will tender that video. We played four seconds, I think, only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, I thought you would take them all together. Madam Registrar, could you please assign number to the four-seconds video.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document video 22533 receives Exhibit Number D1334, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And we'll play this part of the next video, which is 1D5931, from 1:35:21 to 1:35:51.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I asked it to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- yes, from the beginning. Okay, that's fine. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After this, we have General Rose walking around, so we need now to play from 1:41 minutes -- 1 hour, 41 minutes, 49 seconds, up to 1 hour, 43 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't see the time but we can stop here, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It seems to be 1 hour, 42 minutes, 27 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then let's proceed another half minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which tram is this one?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is number 206, the first one that was hit but kept going and stopped near the Sarajevo tobacco factory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We stopped at 1 hour, 43 minutes, and 0 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That was my intention. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your report, we have photograph 140 of tram number 236, the previous one; and photographs 145 and 146 of tram 206. Do you want to see the photographs or can you say something based on the video?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can stay with the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is your conclusion now that you have reviewed the video, the reports by the police and UNPROFOR, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conclusion is that all three events - the shooting at trams 206 and 236 and the shooting at civilians - were involving someone shooting from the Executive Council building.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is the basis of your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MILE POPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is it specifically tram 206, one civilian was hit there and he had the kind of wound that could be inflicted only if the angle of descent is bigger. The maximum angle that we could establish, in terms of the building by the Jewish cemetery, is 5.71 degrees - that's the building that UNPROFOR mentions - and this angle was a lot bigger. So this man was hit in the lip and it ended in the shoulder, and the angle is much bigger; all of this is contained in the report. The top of the tram was hit and then also that corresponds to the wound that he suffered. Then tram 236, it was also hit under an angle that is bigger than the one possible if fire comes from positions of the VRS. UNPROFOR established that on the basis of the traces on the seats and the tram itself, and they determined an angle of 8.41, I think. We've already said that the maximum angle would be 5.70-something, so it's a 3-degree difference. As for the passers-by on the sidewalk between the museum and the Executive Council building, it is obvious on the basis of the traces that dust that goes up to the height of the APC, that fire came from a relatively small distance and the angle was quite big - and that's the only way in which this column of dust could be there. This is confirmed by UNPROFOR reports after the incident. In the grass there they found six craters and they managed to put antenna of radio equipment there, and that shows that the angle was also much bigger than the one that was possible if the fire had come from positions of the VRS. If that had been the case, there only would have been a shallow furrow; an antenna could not stick into it. Practically it would fall on the ground. It would just show a certain direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We've come to the end of our working hours today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we're coming to -- yes, we are at the end. Yes, Mr. Lukic. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you tendering this video-clip?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am tendering this video-clip, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we're now not at the end yet. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D5931 receives Exhibit Number D1335, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there now any clip which was not yet tendered or have we everything in evidence now?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, if I understand things correctly, D1335 subsumes all these --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Both, yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- small clips that we've looked at. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll adjourn for the day. Witness, we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30. You're again instructed not to speak or communicate with whomever about your testimony, whether that is already given or is still to be given. We'd like to see you back tomorrow, Thursday, the 29th of October, 9.30 in the morning. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn until the point in time I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
